claim: Organelle heterogeneity and inter-organelle contacts within a single cell contribute to the limited sensitivity of current organelle separation techniques.
source: Organelle heterogeneity and inter-organelle contacts within a single cell contribute to the limited sensitivity of current organelle separation techniques, thus hindering organelle subpopulation characterization.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a motivation for the study.

claim: DC-iDEP can identify distinct distribution patterns of insulin vesicles from INS-1E insulinoma cells.
source: Here, we use direct current insulator-based dielectrophoresis (DC-iDEP) as an unbiased separation method and demonstrate its capability by identifying distinct distribution patterns of insulin vesicles from INS-1E insulinoma cells.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract.

claim: A significant difference exists in the distribution pattern of insulin vesicles isolated from glucose-stimulated cells relative to unstimulated cells.
source: We observed a significant difference in the distribution pattern of insulin vesicles isolated from glucose-stimulated cells relative to unstimulated cells, in accordance with maturation of vesicles upon glucose stimulation.
evidence: This is a key finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The difference in distribution pattern is indicative of high-resolution separation of vesicle subpopulations.
source: We interpret the difference in distribution pattern to be indicative of high-resolution separation of vesicle subpopulations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results stated in the abstract.

claim: Cell-to-cell heterogeneity of function within a given cell type arises from differences in genomic, epigenomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic components and their subcellular localizations.
source: Cell-to-cell heterogeneity of function within a given cell type arises from differences in genomic, epigenomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic (Goldman et al., 2019) components and their subcellular localizations.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Goldman et al., 2019.

claim: Subpopulations of organelles have been identified for synaptic vesicles.
source: Some examples are subpopulations of organelles as identified for synaptic vesicles (Crawford and Kavalali, 2015), mitochondria (Aryaman et al., 2018), and insulin secretory vesicles (Suckale and Solimena, 2010), among others.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Crawford and Kavalali, 2015.

claim: Subpopulations of organelles have been identified for mitochondria.
source: Some examples are subpopulations of organelles as identified for synaptic vesicles (Crawford and Kavalali, 2015), mitochondria (Aryaman et al., 2018), and insulin secretory vesicles (Suckale and Solimena, 2010), among others.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aryaman et al., 2018.

claim: Subpopulations of organelles have been identified for insulin secretory vesicles.
source: Some examples are subpopulations of organelles as identified for synaptic vesicles (Crawford and Kavalali, 2015), mitochondria (Aryaman et al., 2018), and insulin secretory vesicles (Suckale and Solimena, 2010), among others.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Suckale and Solimena, 2010.

claim: The biochemical composition of different subpopulations of organelles must vary, reflecting differences in age, maturation, or specific biological role.
source: The biochemical composition of each of the different subpopulations of organelles must vary, reflecting differences in age, maturation, or specific biological role.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the concept of organelle subpopulations.

claim: Traditional workflows for organelle isolation consist of iterative centrifugation steps.
source: A traditional workflow consists of iterative centrifugation steps (Harford and Bonifacino, 2011) to isolate populations of targeted organelles for follow-up analysis with mass spectrometric or other omics-scale assays (Huber et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harford and Bonifacino, 2011 and Huber et al., 2003.

claim: Gradient columns have successfully isolated clathrin-coated vesicles based on differences in organelle densities.
source: Gradient columns have successfully isolated clathrin-coated vesicles (Girard et al., 2005), lipid droplets (Brasaemle and Wolins, 2016), mitochondria, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) populations (Bozidis et al., 2007), from other organelles, based on differences in organelle densities.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Girard et al., 2005.

claim: Gradient columns have successfully isolated lipid droplets based on differences in organelle densities.
source: Gradient columns have successfully isolated clathrin-coated vesicles (Girard et al., 2005), lipid droplets (Brasaemle and Wolins, 2016), mitochondria, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) populations (Bozidis et al., 2007), from other organelles, based on differences in organelle densities.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brasaemle and Wolins, 2016.

claim: Gradient columns have successfully isolated mitochondria and endoplasmic reticulum populations based on differences in organelle densities.
source: Gradient columns have successfully isolated clathrin-coated vesicles (Girard et al., 2005), lipid droplets (Brasaemle and Wolins, 2016), mitochondria, and endoplasmic reticulum (ER) populations (Bozidis et al., 2007), from other organelles, based on differences in organelle densities.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bozidis et al., 2007.

claim: Subpopulations of a given organelle with similar buoyant densities are often hard to differentiate and separate in gradient columns.
source: However, subpopulations of a given organelle with similar buoyant densities are often hard to differentiate and separate in these columns.
evidence: This is a limitation of gradient column methods stated in the text.

claim: Immunoisolation of organelles is limited by the need for specific organelle markers.
source: Immunoisolation of organelles, although yielding pure populations, is limited by the need for specific organelle markers (Lange et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lange et al., 2000.

claim: Free-flow electrophoresis has been adopted for use in microfluidic separation of organelles.
source: Electrophoretic approaches, such as free-flow electrophoresis, have been adopted for use in microfluidic separation of organelles (Lu et al., 2004), enabling downstream analyses of the enriched fractions in the absence of major contaminants.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2004.

claim: Free-flow electrophoresis separations are limited to differentiation based on charge and size of the components.
source: However, these separations are limited to differentiation based on charge and size of the components.
evidence: This is a limitation of electrophoretic approaches stated in the text.

claim: Traditional isolation approaches lack sufficient sensitivity and robustness to isolate subpopulations of an organelle for biochemical characterizations except for smooth versus rough ER.
source: Although powerful, each of these traditional isolation approaches lacks sufficient sensitivity and robustness to isolate subpopulations of an organelle for biochemical characterizations such as proteomic analysis or imaging, except for smooth versus rough ER (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a limitation of traditional methods with citation to Lee et al., 2015 for the exception.

claim: DC-iDEP utilizes higher order electric field effects to differentiate bioparticles based on radius, zeta potential, permittivity, interfacial polarizability, charge distribution, deformability, and conductivity.
source: One attractive strategy is to exploit higher order electric field effects which directly probe the nuanced physical properties of small complex bioparticles—differentiating on radius, zeta potential, permittivity, interfacial polarizability, charge distribution, deformability, and conductivity of the particles, to name but a few (Chen et al., 2009; Hilton et al., 2020; Pethig, 2019; Matyushov, 2019; Hayes, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: DC-iDEP has been used for separating subpopulations of viruses, bacteria, organelles, and proteins.
source: Direct current insulator-based dielectrophoresis (DC-iDEP) utilizes these features for separating subpopulations of bioparticles such as viruses, bacteria, organelles, and proteins (Hayes, 2020; Ding et al., 2016; Jones et al., 2015; Liu and Hayes, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: DC-iDEP has been specifically used for separations ranging from neural progenitors and stem cells to resistant versus susceptible strains of cellular pathogens.
source: This approach offers a wide dynamic range, as it has been specifically used for separations ranging from neural progenitors and stem cells (Liu et al., 2019) to resistant versus susceptible strains of cellular pathogens (Hilton et al., 2020; Jones et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2019, Hilton et al., 2020, and Jones et al., 2015.

claim: DC-iDEP is well suited for assaying subpopulations of organelles where differentiating factors are not known.
source: Unlike epitope recognition strategies, DC-iDEP is well suited for assaying subpopulations of organelles, where differentiating factors are not known.
evidence: This is a stated advantage of DC-iDEP in the text.

claim: DC-iDEP can be used as a discovery-based approach to interrogate a broader spectrum of organelle subpopulations.
source: DC-iDEP can be used as a discovery-based approach to interrogate a broader spectrum of organelle subpopulations (Liu et al., 2019) because the bioparticle separations occur quickly and require small sample volume (Kim et al., 2019; Lapizco‐Encinas and Rito‐Palomares, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2019, Kim et al., 2019, and Lapizco-Encinas and Rito-Palomares, 2007.

claim: Pancreatic β-cells are responsible for secreting insulin in a tightly regulated process that is key to maintaining glucose homeostasis.
source: Pancreatic β-cells are responsible for secreting insulin in a tightly regulated process that is key to maintaining glucose homeostasis.
evidence: This is established biological knowledge stated in the text.

claim: Insulin vesicles undergo a complex functional maturation process that is required for proper secretion of insulin.
source: Insulin vesicles undergo a complex functional maturation process that is required for proper secretion of insulin and this process is dysregulated in diabetes (Suckale and Solimena, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Suckale and Solimena, 2010.

claim: The insulin vesicle maturation process is dysregulated in diabetes.
source: Insulin vesicles undergo a complex functional maturation process that is required for proper secretion of insulin and this process is dysregulated in diabetes (Suckale and Solimena, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Suckale and Solimena, 2010.

claim: Immature insulin vesicles act as a sorting compartment.
source: Immature insulin vesicles act as a sorting compartment (Feng and Arvan, 2003; Huang and Arvan, 1994) and mature into two distinct pools of functional vesicles within the cell: the readily releasable pool and the reserve pool (Boland et al., 2017; Orci, 1985; Orci et al., 1986; Dean, 1973; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Feng and Arvan, 2003 and Huang and Arvan, 1994.

claim: Immature insulin vesicles mature into two distinct pools of functional vesicles within the cell: the readily releasable pool and the reserve pool.
source: Immature insulin vesicles act as a sorting compartment (Feng and Arvan, 2003; Huang and Arvan, 1994) and mature into two distinct pools of functional vesicles within the cell: the readily releasable pool and the reserve pool (Boland et al., 2017; Orci, 1985; Orci et al., 1986; Dean, 1973; Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Boland et al., 2017, Orci, 1985, Orci et al., 1986, Dean, 1973, and Figure 1A.

claim: The heterogeneity among subpopulations of insulin vesicles likely arises from the varying stages of the maturation process.
source: The heterogeneity among subpopulations of insulin vesicles (Hou et al., 2009; Michael et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2020) likely arises from the varying stages of the maturation process.
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Hou et al., 2009, Michael et al., 2006, and Zhang et al., 2020.

claim: Insulin vesicle heterogeneity accounts for modifications of insulin vesicle membrane proteins, and variances in their age, mobility, and localization within the cell.
source: This accounts for modifications of insulin vesicle membrane proteins, and variances in their age, mobility, and localization within the cell (Suckale and Solimena, 2010; Hao et al., 2005; Halban, 1982; Gold et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Suckale and Solimena, 2010, Hao et al., 2005, Halban, 1982, and Gold et al., 1982.

claim: The associated biochemical constituents of insulin vesicles have remained elusive in the absence of sensitive isolation approaches.
source: However, the associated biochemical constituents of insulin vesicles have remained elusive in the absence of sensitive isolation approaches.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Several groups have attempted to isolate and characterize insulin vesicles.
source: The importance of insulin vesicles in glucose homeostasis has led several groups to attempt to isolate and characterize the insulin vesicles (Thurmond, 2007; Hutton et al., 1982).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Thurmond, 2007 and Hutton et al., 1982.

claim: There is very little overlap in protein IDs associated with insulin vesicles from different proteomics studies.
source: While these studies and follow-up proteomics analysis of the isolated vesicles Schvartz et al., 2012; Li et al., 2018; Brunner et al., 2007; Hickey et al., 2009 have provided insights into the biochemistry of these vesicles, there's very little overlap in protein IDs associated with these organelles from different studies (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 1B showing a Venn diagram with minimal overlap.

claim: INS-1E cells used in these studies were capable of insulin secretion in response to increasing concentrations of glucose.
source: The INS-1E cells used in these studies were capable of insulin secretion in response to increasing concentrations of glucose (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lower fractions of the density column (9–12) contained the highest insulin content.
source: ELISAs identified that lower fractions of the density column (9–12) contained the highest insulin content (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), the same fractions shown to be enriched in the insulin vesicle marker, synaptotagmin IX, by WB (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and 2B.

claim: Fractions 9-12 of the density column were enriched in the insulin vesicle marker, synaptotagmin IX.
source: ELISAs identified that lower fractions of the density column (9–12) contained the highest insulin content (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), the same fractions shown to be enriched in the insulin vesicle marker, synaptotagmin IX, by WB (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Fractions 9-12 of the density column contained particles of 150–200 nm radius, which corresponds to the known range of insulin vesicles radii.
source: DLS indicated that these fractions contained particles of 150–200 nm radius, which corresponds to the known range of insulin vesicles radii (Olofsson et al., 2002; Greider et al., 1969).
evidence: This is supported by DLS data and citations to Olofsson et al., 2002 and Greider et al., 1969.

claim: The final enriched vesicle sample included some contaminants from unwanted organelles, such as the ER.
source: Although the WB revealed that the final enriched vesicle sample included some contaminants from unwanted organelles, such as the ER (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B), this will not confound the analysis of insulin vesicles in the iDEP device as the fluorescent labeling was targeted only at insulin vesicles.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Isolated insulin vesicles were intact prior to DC-iDEP as verified by fluorescence confocal microscopy showing distinct puncta rather than a diffuse GFP signal.
source: We observed distinct puncta rather than a diffuse GFP signal which indicated that the vesicles were intact and not ruptured.
evidence: This is based on fluorescence microscopy observations described in the text.

claim: Intact vesicles with the expected size and shape were observed using both transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM).
source: We observed intact vesicles with the expected size and shape using both transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by EM images shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Synaptotagmin IX colocalizes with insulin in fluorescence microscopy imaging.
source: Enriched vesicle samples from INS-1E cells were subjected to analysis using DC-iDEP after labeling with insulin vesicle marker synaptotagmin IX (Schvartz et al., 2012; Brunner et al., 2007), which was confirmed to colocalize with insulin in fluorescence microscopy imaging (Figure 2).
evidence: This is supported by colocalization data shown in Figure 2 and citations.

claim: A Pearson's r value of 0.66 was observed for colocalization between insulin and synaptotagmin IX in one cell.
source: Pearson's r value, 0.66 (D) and 0.64 (H).
evidence: This is quantitative data from Figure 2D.

claim: A Pearson's r value of 0.64 was observed for colocalization between insulin and synaptotagmin IX in another cell.
source: Pearson's r value, 0.66 (D) and 0.64 (H).
evidence: This is quantitative data from Figure 2H.

claim: At high voltages (2100 V), all particles were prevented from entering the first gate because DEP forces exceed EK forces.
source: The separation system was operated in a discovery or scanning mode by first applying a high voltage (2100 V, empirically determined, Figure 3) such that all particles were prevented from entering the first gate, because DEP forces exceed EK forces.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method and its physical basis.

claim: The voltage was lowered incrementally (300 V for each step) allowing various subpopulations to enter the separation zone and be sorted along the device according to their specific EKMr values.
source: The voltage was then lowered incrementally (300 V for each step) allowing various subpopulations to enter the separation zone and be sorted along the device according to their specific EKMr values (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

claim: A bolus forms at a gate, corresponding to an EKMr value that is a result of a balance between DEP and EK forces on each particle.
source: A bolus forms at a gate, corresponding to an EKMr value that is a result of a balance between DEP and EK forces on each particle and reflects a complex set of biological, chemical, and biophysical properties of the vesicles (Jones et al., 2015; Hilton and Hayes, 2019; Crowther et al., 2019; Liu and Hayes, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jones et al., 2015, Hilton and Hayes, 2019, Crowther et al., 2019, and Liu and Hayes, 2020.

claim: At an applied voltage of 1800 V, n-insulin vesicles were sensed at EKMr values below 1.5×10^10 V/m^2 in patterns of overlapping subpopulations.
source: At an applied voltage of 1800 V, particles were sensed at EKMr values below 1.5×1010 V/m2 in patterns of overlapping subpopulations (Figure 4A, blue circles).
evidence: This is data from Figure 4A.

claim: At an applied voltage of 1200 V, notable and discernible features of n-insulin vesicle bioparticle distribution are apparent around 1.2×10^10 and 1.8×10^10 V/m^2.
source: Notable and discernible features of bioparticle distribution are apparent around 1.2×1010 and 1.8×1010 V/m2 at an applied voltage of 1200 V (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is data from Figure 4C.

claim: At 900 V, n-insulin vesicles show a similar but attenuated feature of the distribution around 1.2×10^10 V/m^2.
source: Lowering the voltage to 900 V, and redistribution of bioparticles based on adapted properties of the channel, reveals a similar but attenuated feature of the distribution around 1.2×1010 V/m2 (Figure 4D), whereas particles with EKMr values greater than 1.5×1010 V/m2 leave the channel at this voltage.
evidence: This is data from Figure 4D.

claim: At 900 V, redistribution of n-insulin vesicles forms a distinct peak around 5–6×10^9 V/m^2.
source: At this voltage, redistribution of particles, previously retained in overlapping patterns at 1200 V, forms a distinct peak around 5–6×109 V/m2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is data from Figure 4D.

claim: At 600 V, n-insulin vesicles show similar patterns of particle distribution around 5–6×10^9 V/m^2, as well as distinctive patterns around 3–4×10^9 V/m^2.
source: Further lowering the voltage to 600 V shows similar patterns of particle distribution around 5–6×109 V/m2, as well as distinctive patterns around 3–4×109 V/m2 (Figure 4E), while leaving out populations with EKMr values higher than 1.0×1010 V/m2.
evidence: This is data from Figure 4E.

claim: At 1800 V, g-insulin vesicles show distribution of particles at values up to 2.3×10^10 V/m^2 (compared to a maximum value of 1.5×10^10 V/m^2 for the untreated populations).
source: Distribution of particles was observed at values up to 2.3×1010 V/m2 (compared to a maximum value of 1.5×1010 V/m2 for the untreated populations) (Figure 4A), which suggests that these vesicles have a broader range of properties than the population from the untreated cells.
evidence: This is data from Figure 4A with an interpretation.

claim: g-insulin vesicles have a broader range of properties than the population from the untreated cells.
source: Distribution of particles was observed at values up to 2.3×1010 V/m2 (compared to a maximum value of 1.5×1010 V/m2 for the untreated populations) (Figure 4A), which suggests that these vesicles have a broader range of properties than the population from the untreated cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the broader distribution range observed in Figure 4A.

claim: At 1500 V, the first evidence of a distinct distribution feature for g-insulin vesicles was captured around 7–8×10^9 V/m^2.
source: The first evidence of a distinct distribution feature was captured around 7–8×109 V/m2 when the voltage was lowered to 1500 V (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is data from Figure 4B.

claim: At 1200 V, g-insulin vesicles show a distribution pattern with discernible features around 7–8×10^9 V/m^2 and a distinct peak around 1.1×10^10 V/m^2.
source: Decreasing the voltage to 1200 V and subsequent particle redistribution in the channel revealed a distribution pattern with discernible features around 7–8×109 V/m2, like those observed at 1500 V, as well as a distinct peak around 1.1×1010 V/m2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is data from Figure 4C.

claim: At 900 V, g-insulin vesicles show a unique distribution pattern with discernible features around 1.1×10^10 V/m^2, 8×10^9 V/m^2, and a peak around 4×10^9 V/m^2.
source: Further lowering the voltage to 900 V resulted in a unique distribution pattern with discernible features around 1.1×1010 V/m2 (Figure 4D), similar to 1200 V, and 8×109 V/m2 (Figure 4D), previously observed at 1500 and 1200 V (Figure 4B and C). Another feature of this distribution pattern was a peak around 4×109 V/m2 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is data from Figure 4D.

claim: At 600 V, g-insulin vesicles show a distribution pattern with features around 4×10^9 and 8×10^9 V/m^2.
source: Ultimately, decreasing the voltage to 600 V revealed a distribution pattern with features around 4×109 and 8×109 V/m2 (Figure 4E), like those observed at higher voltages, leaving out patterns that were observed at EKMr values higher than 1.0×1010 V/m2.
evidence: This is data from Figure 4E.

claim: At 1200 V, there is a statistically significant interaction between the effect of treatment on vesicles collected at each EKMr value (F(8, 45)=3.61, p=0.003).
source: Using a two-way ANOVA, we found a statistically significant interaction between the effect of treatment on vesicles collected at each EKMr value for data collected only at 1200 V (F(8, 45)=3.61, p=0.003).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result.

claim: At 1200 V, there is a significant difference in the intensity or quantity of vesicles collected between treated and untreated samples at 1.10×10^9 V/m^2 (p=0.0249).
source: A Bonferroni post hoc test revealed a significant difference in the intensity or quantity of vesicles collected between treated and untreated samples at 1.10×109 V/m2 (p=0.0249), 5.35×109 V/m2 (p=0.0469), 7.45×109 V/m2 (p=0.0369).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result.

claim: At 1200 V, there is a significant difference in the intensity or quantity of vesicles collected between treated and untreated samples at 5.35×10^9 V/m^2 (p=0.0469).
source: A Bonferroni post hoc test revealed a significant difference in the intensity or quantity of vesicles collected between treated and untreated samples at 1.10×109 V/m2 (p=0.0249), 5.35×109 V/m2 (p=0.0469), 7.45×109 V/m2 (p=0.0369).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result.

claim: At 1200 V, there is a significant difference in the intensity or quantity of vesicles collected between treated and untreated samples at 7.45×10^9 V/m^2 (p=0.0369).
source: A Bonferroni post hoc test revealed a significant difference in the intensity or quantity of vesicles collected between treated and untreated samples at 1.10×109 V/m2 (p=0.0249), 5.35×109 V/m2 (p=0.0469), 7.45×109 V/m2 (p=0.0369).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result.

claim: The differences in vesicle collection between treated and untreated samples reflect a shift in the populations of insulin vesicles upon glucose stimulation.
source: These differences reflect a shift in the populations of insulin vesicles upon glucose stimulation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results.

claim: Different distribution patterns for insulin vesicles isolated from glucose-stimulated versus unstimulated cells suggest glucose stimulation alters the insulin vesicle subpopulations.
source: Furthermore, we observed different distribution patterns for insulin vesicles isolated from glucose-stimulated versus unstimulated cells, which suggests glucose stimulation alters the insulin vesicle subpopulations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed distribution patterns.

claim: The observed differences in insulin vesicle distribution patterns are consistent with findings from single-cell soft X-ray tomography, which revealed heterogeneities in the composition of insulin vesicles and their molecular densities upon glucose stimulation due to vesicle maturation.
source: This is consistent with findings from single-cell soft X-ray tomography, which revealed heterogeneities in the composition of insulin vesicles and their molecular densities upon glucose stimulation due to vesicle maturation (White et al., 2020; Loconte et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to White et al., 2020 and Loconte et al., 2022.

claim: Other studies have observed enrichment of certain subpopulations of vesicles in response to glucose stimulation.
source: Other studies have also observed enrichment of certain subpopulations of vesicles in response to glucose stimulation (Straub et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Straub et al., 2004.

claim: The intensity peaks observed at specific EKMr values likely correspond to some of the previously described insulin vesicle subpopulations.
source: The intensity peaks we observed at specific EKMr values likely correspond to some of the previously described insulin vesicle subpopulations (Zhang et al., 2020; Norris et al., 2021; Neukam et al., 2020; Yau et al., 2020; Kreutzberger et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2020, Norris et al., 2021, Neukam et al., 2020, Yau et al., 2020, and Kreutzberger et al., 2020.

claim: Larger particles are expected to have a smaller EKMr value compared to smaller particles.
source: Larger particles are expected to have a smaller EKMr value compared to smaller particles (Hilton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hilton et al., 2020.

claim: Subpopulations containing larger insulin vesicles, such as a mature pool, synaptotagmin IX-positive vesicles, or docked vesicles near the plasma membrane may have lower EKMr values than smaller immature vesicles.
source: Subpopulations containing larger insulin vesicles, such as a mature pool (Zhang et al., 2020; Norris et al., 2021), synaptotagmin IX-positive vesicles (Kreutzberger et al., 2020), or docked vesicles near the plasma membrane (Zhang et al., 2020) may have lower EKMr values than smaller immature vesicles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between particle size and EKMr, supported by citations.

claim: Phosphatidylcholine lipids increase the zeta potential of tristearoylglycerol crystals.
source: Additionally, phosphatidylcholine lipids increase the zeta potential of tristearoylglycerol crystals (Arts et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Arts et al., 1994.

claim: The effect of phosphatidylcholine on zeta potential may extend to insulin vesicle subpopulations containing more phosphatidylcholine, such as young insulin vesicles, which could lead to higher EKMr values.
source: This effect may extend to insulin vesicle subpopulations containing more phosphatidylcholine, such as young insulin vesicles (Neukam et al., 2020) which could lead to higher EKMr values.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effect of phosphatidylcholine on zeta potential, supported by citation to Neukam et al., 2020.

claim: Insulin vesicles with EKMr values of 1–2×10^9 V/m^2 may represent a synaptotagmin IX-positive subpopulation due to their larger radii and depletion under glucose stimulation.
source: For example, insulin vesicles with EKMr values of 1–2×109 V/m2 (Figure 4C) may represent a synaptotagmin IX-positive subpopulation due to their larger radii and depletion under glucose stimulation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data in Figure 4C.

claim: Young insulin vesicles may have EKMr values between 5 and 7.5×10^9 V/m^2 due to higher amounts of phosphatidylcholine present in this subpopulation.
source: Additionally, young insulin vesicles may have EKMr values between 5 and 7.5×109 V/m2 (Figure 4C) due to higher amounts of phosphatidylcholine present in this subpopulation (Neukam et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the data in Figure 4C and citation to Neukam et al., 2020.

claim: In the EKMr range of 5-7.5×10^9 V/m^2, a higher intensity was observed for glucose-treated cells which may suggest biosynthesis of new vesicles.
source: In this EKMr range, we observed a higher intensity for glucose-treated cells which may suggest biosynthesis of new vesicles.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed data.

claim: Immature insulin vesicles are likely to have higher EKMr values due to their smaller size, such as an EKMr value between 1.5 and 1.6×10^10 V/m^2.
source: Immature insulin vesicles are likely to have higher EKMr values due to their smaller size (Zhang et al., 2020), such as an EKMr value between 1.5 and 1.6×1010 V/m2 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between particle size and EKMr, supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2020 and data in Figure 4C.

claim: The intensity at each EKMr value is influenced by individual insulin vesicles.
source: The intensity at each EKMr value is influenced by individual insulin vesicles.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of the data.

claim: The distribution of the intensity pattern reflects differences in physical properties of the vesicles such as physical changes to the vesicles as they mature.
source: The distribution of this pattern reflects differences in physical properties of the vesicles such as physical changes to the vesicles as they mature.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed distribution patterns.

claim: The specific changes to the individual insulin vesicles which result in varied EKMr measurements can be associated with any alteration of the biochemical makeup of the bioparticle.
source: The specific changes to the individual insulin vesicles which result in varied EKMr measurements can be associated with any alteration of the biochemical makeup of the bioparticle.
evidence: This is a statement about the interpretation of EKMr measurements.

claim: The overall structure and subtle details of the bioparticle, including the particle-solvent cross-polarizations, will influence DEP and EK forces.
source: It is becoming better understood that the overall structure and subtle details of the bioparticle, including the particle-solvent cross-polarizations, will influence these forces (Pethig, 2019; Matyushov, 2019; Hayes, 2020; Hölzel and Pethig, 2021; Martin and Matyushov, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pethig, 2019, Matyushov, 2019, Hayes, 2020, Hölzel and Pethig, 2021, and Martin and Matyushov, 2012.

claim: The makeup of the insulin vesicle has changed: something has been added, subtracted, or altered which changed the force on the particle in a measurable and quantifiable way.
source: This new view of the forces imparted on the insulin vesicles aligns with a rather simple proposition that the makeup of the particle has changed: something has been added, subtracted, or altered which changed the force on the particle in a measurable and quantifiable way.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed changes in EKMr values.

claim: Glucose can affect the maturation of existing vesicles, increasing their molecular density or the concentration of biomolecules within the vesicle lumen.
source: This is consistent with findings that glucose can affect the maturation of existing vesicles, increasing their molecular density or the concentration of biomolecules within the vesicle lumen (White et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to White et al., 2020.

evidence: This is a description of the cell culture method.

evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.

evidence: This is a description of the experimental method.
